issues: The latitude is wrong by one degree. The record gives lat 38.8052, which is in the Sierra foothills. Downtown Oakland, where the California DOJ office at 1515 Clay Street stands, is at about 37.805 N, -122.273 W. The corrected latitude is 37.8052.

'It was the first publicly disclosed CCPA settlement' is overstated. Private class-action settlements that included CCPA data-breach claims came before August 2022. The sources support something narrower. The AG's own DoorDash release of 21 February 2024 says 'Today’s settlement with DoorDash marks Attorney General Bonta’s second CCPA enforcement settlement'. Arnold & Porter call it the 'second publicly disclosed settlement by the OAG'. The summary now says it was the Attorney General's first publicly disclosed CCPA enforcement settlement.

The summary said the AG sent notices to businesses 'that were not processing such signals', which states allegations as fact. The release says the notices were 'alleging non-compliance'. The same applies to the title: Sephora settled allegations and did not admit to ignoring GPC. The title and summary are reworded to say this.

Everything else is confirmed on a fresh fetch. Both OAG quotes are verbatim. The release is dated Wednesday, August 24, 2022 (dc:date 2022-08-24) and datelined OAKLAND. The $1.2 million penalty and the injunctive term to provide an opt-out 'including via the Global Privacy Control' are on the page.
Arnold & Porter source: the quote is verbatim, and the page date is April 15, 2024, not just '2024-04'.

fieldFixes.title: Sephora pays $1.2 million to settle claims it ignored Global Privacy Control
fieldFixes.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced a settlement with Sephora resolving allegations that it failed to disclose that it sold consumers' personal information, failed to process opt-out requests sent via user-enabled global privacy controls, and did not cure these violations within the 30-day period the CCPA then allowed. Sephora agreed to pay $1.2 million in penalties and to provide ways for consumers to opt out of sale, including via the Global Privacy Control; the same day the Attorney General sent notices to other businesses alleging that they were failing to process such signals. It was the Attorney General's first publicly disclosed CCPA enforcement settlement; the second, with DoorDash, came in February 2024.

issues: The summary said Executive Order 14086 created a Data Protection Review Court. The decision itself says the redress mechanism 'is established, under EO 14086, complemented by the AG Regulation establishing the Data Protection Review Court' (28 CFR part 201). So the court was established by the Attorney General's regulation, not by the EO itself. The summary is corrected.

The significance called it 'The third transatlantic arrangement in eight years', which is wrong. The three arrangements are Safe Harbor (2000), Privacy Shield (2016) and the DPF (2023), spread over 23 years. What happened within eight years was two replacements after Safe Harbor was struck down in 2015. The significance is corrected.

Source [1] quote is recital 7, not an operative article. It is also cut off mid-sentence before 'to certified organisations in the United States.' The operative adequacy finding is Article 1, and the summary's wording ('organisations certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework') paraphrases Article 1. The quote is replaced with Article 1.
Also confirmed: recital 6 quote is verbatim; 'Done at Brussels, 10 July 2023'; OJ L 231/118, 20.9.2023; document C(2023)4745. The Berlaymont coordinates are about right.

fieldFixes.summary: After Schrems II, the United States adopted Executive Order 14086 on 7 October 2022, setting new limits and safeguards on signals-intelligence activities and a new redress mechanism for Europeans, complemented by an Attorney General regulation establishing a Data Protection Review Court. On 10 July 2023 the Commission adopted Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795, finding that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred from the Union to organisations on the Data Privacy Framework List kept by the US Department of Commerce.
fieldFixes.significance: The third transatlantic arrangement since 2000 — and the second replacement in eight years after the Court of Justice struck down Safe Harbor in 2015 — it shows how contested the legal plumbing under every data flow remains, and why terms that travel with the person, not the pipe, are attractive.
